title: Is there any trading guide for Ai agent???
author: No_Car1901
selftext:
Well i have tried many repos to train AI agent. None has workout with over 50% Success rate...

So going blindly with any repo is not the solution as far as i could crack it. Though, I have modified and introduced some new logics with it to understand market better. It has impacted its working but not satisfactory results i got so far.

So, I have been thinking if there is some guide which can train Ai agents from the very basics.

Drop down ur ideas guys..!!

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
honestly there's no guide that turns an AI agent into a profitable trader, and anyone selling one is selling the guide, not the profits. a few things I learned the hard way though:

win rate over 50% isn't the goal. you can win 70% of trades and still lose money if the losers are bigger. look at average win vs average loss, after fees.

if the agent is an LLM, you can't backtest it properly. it has already seen the price history it's being tested on, so the results look way better than they are. only forward results on new data count.

what worked better for me was using AI to write and check code, not to make the trading decisions. pick one simple idea, write it as plain rules, then compare it against random entries with the same holding time and fees. if it can't beat random, more AI on top won't fix it, it just finds a fancier way to overfit.

and be careful with apps that pop up in the comments offering "AI analysis" of your data, reddit is full of them.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
Tbh I'd stop switching repos for a while. Pick one, and before changing any logic, compare it to something dumb like buy and hold or random entries with the same fees, on data it never saw.

Also 50% success rate isn't really the target. A 40% win rate can make money if the winners are bigger, and 70% can still lose. Look at average win vs average loss after fees.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body:
450 dry runs is a decent amount to look at. One thing I'd check: does the dry run P&L line up with what the backtest says for the same days? If they drift apart, it's usually fills or fees, not the logic.

And I'd keep the LLM as the one that warns you, not the one that changes settings. It's good at explaining what broke, not so good at knowing when it's wrong 🙃

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
a guide won't fix it. most of those repos teach an agent to fit the past and then grade it on the same past, so the score means nothing. what matters is the loop around the agent: it writes one rule, the rule is checked on dates it never saw, and only what survives gets kept.

Quantradin runs that loop. I built it in June: your own AI plugs in, writes a stock rule, and has it checked on unseen dates before it trades pretend money. quantradin.com. what is your agent trading, stocks or crypto?

comments.author: Reasonable_Comb3171
comments.body: If the agent works they wouldn’t be selling it. Walk in step with AI don’t move to fast or you’ll drown in features and add one that you don’t even understand. If you understand how it works then you know how to adapt it. Get a baseline which is what I’m doing now then move from there. I think the best move is to let the ideas come to you slowly put out a V1 and test test test. Patience is key. Know when your restricting the models capability or enhancing it based on results. From my observation restricting the model to a small 1,000.00 paper account with a 25/0/30 trailing stop as my only fixed rule has prompted interesting results. It really fights for results in such a tight paper account. My max risk is set to 50% of the account. I feel that if you get too lost in the weeds with setting fixed rule parameters you’ll choke the agent on certain days versus others. My stuff is still to young to tell it’s results compared to a coin flip. This is just my two cents. It’s important to to note that this will take a while and be hesitant with trusting your results, take some lessons the model learned and backtest them without an agent running to see if you break even and save money typically you won’t see rule based trades net positive from what I’ve seen in backtests, part of the idea with the agents fluid rules is to allow it to discern its past choices if you tell it “you have to do this and this” it will without question most times.

comments.author: TrenchersAi
comments.body:
agree with the comment above on win rate. one thing that helped me more than any repo: stop trying to train the agent to "understand the market" and start with a dumb rule set you can explain in one sentence.

1. define the entry in plain rules first (volume, liquidity, holder spread, whatever your edge is). if you can't write it down, the agent can't learn it either.

2. hard-code the risk side. max position size, stop loss, max trades per day. don't let the model decide these.

3. log every exit with a reason (stop hit, take profit, time out). after 50+ trades you'll see which rule is actually losing money.

4. run it forward on small size or simulated funds for a few weeks before trusting any number.

most agents don't fail on entries, they fail on exits and sizing. what market are you running it on?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: A success rate under 50% isn't automatically bad, since what counts is the win rate against the break-even rate once you know your average win, average loss and fees. A strategy that wins 40% of the time can still make money if the winners are bigger than the losers. Before adding more logic to a repo, I'd test a simple baseline like random entries or buy and hold on the same data, so you know what the agent has to beat. Then keep a recent stretch of data that you never tune on. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and can hold out the last part of the history, which fits that kind of check.

comments.author: eduard_trades
comments.body:
I'd question the 50% target first. Win rate on its own says almost nothing about whether a strategy makes money.



A system that wins 40% of the time can be profitable if winners are twice the size of losers. One that wins 70% can lose money if it takes small profits and lets losses run. I had exactly that in my own tests: one exit version had a higher win rate than the other and a lower profit per trade, because it booked many small wins and gave back more on the losers.



What to measure instead: average result per trade after fees, in units of your risk (R). If that's not clearly above zero over a few hundred trades, the win rate doesn't matter.



On guides: no repo will hand you an edge, because anything that works and gets published stops working. What you can learn from guides is how to test honestly. Compare every version against random entries with the same exits and costs, decide the pass threshold before you look at results, and keep data you never tuned on for the final check. That's what tells you whether your changes improve anything or just fit the past.
